d_notes.title: Designer Notes
d_notes.description: This portfolio was designed to balance contemporary web presentation with subtle references to early web aesthetics, using structure, typography, and interaction to guide the user experience.

process.intent: The project explores how structure, hierarchy, and interaction design can shape user perception. By combining a vertical navigation system with minimal motion and editorial layout principles, the goal was to create an experience that feels both structured and interactive without overwhelming the user.
decisions: Vertical navigation was used to maintain spatial consistency and reinforce a clear structural hierarchy across sections.
A muted color palette was selected to reduce cognitive load and allow layout and typography to guide attention.
Background textures were kept subtle to introduce depth without competing with primary content.
Minimal transitions were applied to keep the focus on content while still providing feedback during interaction.
Interactive elements were introduced selectively to add personality without disrupting usability.

gallery.title: Initial Portfolio Sketch
gallery.description: This initial sketch explored layout hierarchy and spatial relationships between navigation, hero content, and supporting sections.

gallery.title: Layout Variations
gallery.description: These variations explored a single-page structure where users can navigate between sections fluidly, reducing friction and avoiding unnecessary page transitions.

gallery.title: Interaction Concept
gallery.description: The interaction model was designed to balance clarity and engagement, introducing subtle motion and feedback without overwhelming the user.

gallery.title: Navigation System
gallery.description: The vertical navigation system reinforces structure and hierarchy while allowing users to move between sections efficiently without losing context within the layout.

gallery.title: Visual Design & Implementation Flow
gallery.description: This diagram shows how the website structure moves from planning into HTML, CSS, JavaScript, version control, and deployment.

gallery.title: 404 Experience
gallery.description: The 404 page extends the visual system into edge cases. Motion and subtle visual changes were used to reduce friction and transform a potential dead-end into a more engaging moment.

projects.title: Uncle Boojie's
projects.subtitle: Divi
projects.headline: Five pages, five ways to make content easier to read
projects.tagline: I designed five pages for Uncle Boojie's website, each with a different kind of content, from an editorial page and a long blog post to an eleven-chapter document, the Experience page and a cocktail recipe book.
projects.summary: Website work for Uncle Boojie's, a Kentucky business that offers bourbon tastings, a brunch with Highland cows and a series of signature experiences. Five pages designed in Divi during my internship at Andrew Kung Group, each with its own content and its own design decisions.

description.text: During my internship at Andrew Kung Group, I designed five pages for Uncle Boojie's website. Each one had a different kind of content: an editorial page, a long blog post, a long-form document with eleven chapters, the Experience page and a cocktail recipe book. Each one needed its own answer to the same question: how do I make this content easier to read, follow and act on?

impact.text: Across the five pages, the content became easier to scan, follow and act on, with one consistent visual system across desktop, tablet and mobile. For me, the project was real practice in working inside an existing site and within a client's rules: using only the client's existing text, documenting every decision, and presenting versions for approval before building the final one.

features: Magazine-style editorial layout with captioned images
Chart and highlighted phrases for a long blog post
Side menu and accordion for an eleven-chapter document
Card system and pre-filled request form for the Experience page
Consistent button system across pages
Recipe cards that open on the photo, with download and share

chapters.page: The Lifeblood of an Isolated Community
chapters.label: Editorial layout
chapters.intro: A content page designed like a magazine spread.

decisions.title: A magazine layout for a long page
decisions.why: I organized the page like a magazine spread, so a long page reads in visual steps instead of one continuous block.

decisions.title: Every image placed with its own text
decisions.why: I paired each image with the paragraph it belongs to and gave each one a caption, so the images help tell the story instead of just decorating it.

chapters.label: Historical post
chapters.intro: A long historical post on how federal taxes, raids and Prohibition-era poisonings affected Kentucky's whiskey makers.

decisions.title: A chart that makes the numbers visible
decisions.why: The federal whiskey tax rose tenfold in three years. An animated chart lets the reader see that jump instead of reading it in a paragraph, and because it's built in HTML/CSS rather than as an image, it scales cleanly on mobile.

decisions.title: Highlighted phrases
decisions.why: Key phrases are pulled out and highlighted, giving readers points to rest and making the main ideas easy to find while scanning.

chapters.page: Why Do You Keep Calling My Whisky Bourbon?
chapters.label: Long-form content
chapters.intro: An introduction, conclusions and eleven chapters, each with a different type of content.

decisions.title: Where the page started
decisions.why: The content came as a PDF file with images that needed to be transferred to a web page. I thought about ways to present the information that would keep it easy to read and also interesting.

decisions.title: A side menu on desktop, an accordion on mobile
decisions.why: On desktop, a side menu keeps all eleven chapters one click away and shows one at a time. On mobile, where a side menu doesn't fit, the same chapters become an accordion: the page stays short at first glance and readers open only what they want to read.

decisions.title: Each chapter designed for its content
decisions.why: Some chapters had many images, others only text, others a lot of text and few images. I designed each one for what it had to show instead of forcing one template on all eleven, and also designed the introduction and conclusions.

chapters.label: Booking experiences
chapters.intro: Eight experiences, each with its own price, details and way to book.

decisions.title: Where the page started
decisions.why: The Experience page already presented everything Uncle Boojie's offers. My goal was to make it work even better, so guests could compare every option at a glance and take the next step easily, especially on mobile. I started by sketching the new structure in Excalidraw before building it in Divi.

decisions.title: Cards to compare at a glance
decisions.why: A two-level card system: the main experiences first, then the six signature experiences in a grid that becomes a swipe carousel on mobile. The buttons stay consistent with the rest of the site: outline as the standard, solid gold only for the main action inside each card.

decisions.title: A request form that fills itself in
decisions.why: The form opens on the same page with the selected experience already written in, so guests don't have to type it or leave the page.

decisions.title: The original text, reorganized to be read
decisions.why: I didn't write new copy. The long invitation text was split across the invitation, the Single Barrel card and the closing section, and its strongest line became the closing headline, so the same words are now read instead of skipped.

chapters.label: Recipe book
chapters.intro: Twelve house cocktails, presented as a recipe book that leads to the shop and to the Homeplace.

decisions.title: Two directions, one choice
decisions.why: The recipes were published as images. Moving them into text makes each one searchable, readable by screen readers and easy to share on its own. I sketched two directions for the client, an editorial layout and a recipe book, and she chose the recipe book: the story at the top and the cocktails below.

decisions.title: The recipe opens on the photo
decisions.why: Tapping a photo shows its recipe on top of it, at the same size as the image, so the grid stays clean and nobody leaves the page. Each recipe links to the products used in it, so the page works as a quiet path to the shop.

decisions.title: Cocktails first on mobile
decisions.why: On mobile, the story is cut short with "Read more" so the cocktails show up right away. The name sits above each photo, and the photos switch to a taller format so the full recipe fits inside.

decisions.title: Find a cocktail without distractions
decisions.why: A dropdown opens the chosen recipe in a pop-up, for visitors who already know what they're looking for.

decisions.title: A recipe you can keep and share
decisions.why: A download button turns the recipe, as it's published on the site, into an image with the logo and the web address, so a saved recipe always matches the website and still says where it came from. A share button sends a direct link that opens the page with that recipe already open.

decisions.title: Two ways to go further
decisions.why: After the recipes, the page offers the products used in them and an invitation to Shakers & Thieves, for visitors who would rather taste the cocktails than make them.

projects.title: Hiraldo Wood Resin
projects.subtitle: WordPress
projects.tagline: Online store and custom-order flow for a live-edge wood and resin artist.
projects.cardStack: This is a live client project currently in its final phase, and that product photography is pending the client's photographer, so some visuals shown are placeholders for demonstration purposes.
projects.summary: Custom WooCommerce build for a live-edge wood and resin artist, combining a dynamic design library, a multi-step customization form, and a fully custom design system. This is a live client project currently in its final phase, and product photography is pending the client's photographer, so some visuals shown are placeholders for demonstration purposes.

description.text: This project is a full e-commerce and custom-commission website for a woodworking and resin artist. Beyond a standard WooCommerce shop, the build includes a dynamic 'Design Library' where customers can select existing sketches and carry that reference directly into a multi-step customization request, plus a fully documented design system covering color, typography, and reusable components.

challenge.text: The client's needs evolved significantly mid-project: an initial 'completed work' gallery had to be rebuilt into a 'Design Library' where each sketch links directly into the customization form, carrying the selected design's title and image as context. This required connecting two separate custom post types and forms through URL parameters and JavaScript, while avoiding duplicate script execution across pages that share form field names. A second challenge was styling deeply nested WooCommerce and form plugin markup, which required resolving CSS specificity conflicts against third-party plugin styles rather than relying on simple class overrides.

solution.text: A custom PHP shortcode queries a dedicated 'sketches' post type and renders each design with a button that passes its title and image URL as query parameters to the customization form. A scoped JavaScript snippet reads those parameters, pre-fills the message field, displays a visual reference above it, and appends the reference link at submission time without ever showing it to the user. Each script checks for its target form's unique ID before running, preventing cross-page conflicts. On the styling side, a full design system was built from a client-approved color and typography reference, using CSS custom properties for a single source of truth, with targeted high-specificity selectors to override WooCommerce Blocks and Forminator's default styles consistently across desktop and mobile.

impact.text: The final site gives the client a clear, scalable way to showcase available designs and convert interest directly into a structured quote request, reducing back-and-forth communication before a project even starts. The design system means future style changes only need to happen in one place, and the responsive fixes ensure the experience holds up across devices despite the site's complexity.

features: Dynamic Design Library connected to a custom quote form
Multi-step conditional customization form
Custom design system with reusable CSS components
Cross-page reference passing via URL parameters
Responsive layout across shop, gallery, and forms

projects.title: InvenTrack
projects.subtitle: Web Application
projects.tagline: Inventory app that brings printers, supplies, equipment, sales and loans into one system.
projects.cardStack: An inventory management application designed to bring printer monitoring, supplies, equipment, consumables, sales, loans, maintenance, locations, and reporting into one connected operational system.
projects.summary: A multi-module inventory management application that I have been developing iteratively using Base44. I used the platform's AI-assisted building capabilities to turn a complex set of inventory requirements into a functional system with connected modules, operational workflows, reporting, mobile behavior, and a dashboard focused on actionable information.

description.text: InvenTrack started as an inventory-management concept and gradually expanded as I identified more relationships and operational needs. I defined how the different areas of the system should work together, including Printer Models, individual Printer Units, ink and replacement supplies, Consumables, Equipment, Tablets, Locations, Sales, Loans, maintenance, and reporting. Rather than treating every area as an isolated inventory table, I worked on creating clear responsibilities and relationships between them so the application could function as one connected system.

challenge.text: The biggest challenge was managing the growing complexity of the application without allowing the same information to become duplicated across multiple modules. As the project evolved, I had to decide what information belonged to reference data, what staff needed for daily operations, what should exist only as transaction history, and what should appear only in reports. For example, Printer Models define the supplies a model uses, while Printer Units represent the individual physical printers and their current supply conditions. Tablets remain individual inventory records while Loans store borrowing transactions over time. Sales reference existing Consumables instead of creating a separate sales inventory. I also had to continually reorganize the navigation and dashboard as the number of entities and workflows increased.

solution.text: I used Base44 as the implementation platform and worked through the application in iterative rounds, defining requirements, testing the resulting behavior, identifying problems, and refining the system. I reorganized the information architecture into operational modules, reports, and setup/reference data; defined relationships between inventory records and transactions; established status and alert logic; and redesigned the Today dashboard around the principle of summary, problem, and action. I also specified workflows for printer supply monitoring, replacement-stock availability, consumable sales, tablet lending and returns, equipment maintenance, location tracking, filtering, search, reporting, and responsive mobile use. Because I worked primarily within Base44's available AI credits, features often had to be prioritized and grouped carefully before each implementation round.

impact.text: The result is a functional application with multiple connected entities instead of a collection of disconnected inventory tables. Staff can identify printers requiring attention, compare installed supply needs with replacement stock, manage consumables and equipment, record sales, track tablet loans and returns, monitor maintenance, search inventory, and access detailed reports from the same system. For me, the project became an extended exercise in product thinking: taking a broad operational problem, breaking it into manageable systems, defining how those systems should communicate, testing the experience, and continuously refining it as new requirements emerged.

features: Operational dashboard focused on urgent issues and quick actions
Printer Models connected to individual physical Printer Units
Structured printer ink, toner, and supply-level monitoring
Replacement supply inventory connected to printer needs
Consumable inventory with sales and automatic stock updates
Tablet inventory with loan and return transaction history
Equipment and maintenance tracking
Location-based asset organization
Cross-category inventory and supply reports
Search, filtering, status indicators, and actionable alerts
Responsive workflows for desktop and mobile use

projects.title: J&G Photography
projects.subtitle: Coded
projects.tagline: Photography studio website that guides visitors from the gallery to booking.
projects.summary: Custom-coded photography website focused on service presentation, gallery structure, and user flow.

description.text: This project is a custom-coded website for a photography business. The goal was to create a structure that prioritizes clarity without losing the emotional impact of the imagery. The design focuses on guiding the user through services, galleries, and booking options in a way that feels natural rather than overwhelming.

challenge.text: The main challenge was organizing multiple photography services while maintaining a calm and visually driven experience. Photography websites often rely heavily on imagery, which can easily disrupt navigation and hierarchy. The goal was to balance strong visual content with clear structure, ensuring users could explore without feeling lost and always have a clear path toward booking or contact.

solution.text: The layout was designed to guide the user progressively rather than presenting everything at once. Services are introduced as visual entry points, allowing users to choose based on context instead of reading long descriptions. A masonry-style gallery was implemented to accommodate different image proportions. Instead of forcing consistency through cropping, the layout preserves the integrity of each photograph, creating a more organic visual rhythm. The package customization system was structured to reduce cognitive load by revealing options only after a selection is made. This prevents users from mixing choices across packages and keeps the decision process focused and controlled.

impact.text: The final result provides a structured and intuitive experience that supports both exploration and decision-making. Users can quickly understand the type of services offered, engage with the photography style, and move toward booking without unnecessary friction. The design reinforces trust by keeping the experience simple, guided, and visually consistent.

projects.title: Handyman DMD
projects.subtitle: WordPress
projects.tagline: Service business website built around trust and quick access to contact.
projects.summary: Service-based website focused on clarity, trust, and fast access to key actions.

description.text: This project focuses on translating a hands-on service business into a clear and trustworthy digital experience. The goal was to remove friction from the user journey by prioritizing immediate understanding of services and direct access to contact actions. Every design decision supports clarity over decoration, ensuring users can quickly recognize what is offered and how to take the next step.

challenge.text:
The business offers multiple services, which can easily overwhelm users if not structured carefully. The challenge was to present all information clearly while maintaining a sense of simplicity and trust.

To approach this, early layout sketches were used to explore how services, navigation, and call-to-action elements should be organized. This step helped define a clear hierarchy before moving into the final interface, ensuring that information would guide the user instead of competing for attention.

solution.text: The solution focuses on structured simplicity. Content was grouped into clear service categories, supported by a consistent visual hierarchy that directs attention from overview to action. Navigation was simplified to reduce cognitive load, while custom CSS adjustments refined spacing, typography, and visual rhythm. The design intentionally avoids unnecessary elements, allowing key actions like contacting or requesting services to remain highly visible.

impact.text: The final result is a more focused and reliable user experience that improves how services are understood and how users interact with the site. By reducing visual noise and reinforcing clear pathways, the design supports faster decision-making and builds trust through consistency and clarity.

projects.title: JLPrezc Portfolio
projects.subtitle: Coded
projects.tagline: Dark photography portfolio that keeps the focus on the images.
projects.summary: Dark photography portfolio designed to keep the focus on image presentation.

description.text: This project explores how to present a large body of photography without overwhelming the viewer. The primary decision was to reduce visual noise and let the images carry the experience. A dark interface was not only a stylistic choice, but a functional one, used to control contrast, guide attention, and create a consistent viewing environment across different image types.

challenge.text: The main challenge was not just the number of images, but how they are perceived when presented together. Large image sets can quickly become visually chaotic if hierarchy is not controlled. The problem became defining how much content to show at once, how to group images meaningfully, and how to maintain focus without restricting exploration.

solution.text: The gallery was designed as a controlled system rather than a simple grid. Instead of displaying all images at once, the layout limits initial exposure and allows expansion when needed. This reduces cognitive load while still supporting a large volume of content. The masonry-style arrangement preserves the natural proportions of the images, avoiding forced cropping and maintaining visual integrity. Interaction patterns such as overlays and progressive reveal were used to give users control without adding visual clutter.

impact.text: The final result is a gallery experience that feels organized without being rigid. Images remain the primary focus while the system behind them provides structure and flow. The design supports both quick browsing and deeper exploration, reflecting a balance between visual impact and usability.

projects.title: Aurora Wellness Center
projects.subtitle: WordPress
projects.tagline: Brand and website concept for a calm, cohesive wellness center.
projects.summary: Wellness website case study focused on visual consistency, calm interaction, and brand alignment.

description.text: This project is a conceptual wellness website developed as part of a design course. The goal was to approach it as a real-world scenario, creating a complete brand and web experience from scratch rather than redesigning an existing product. Every decision was made with the intention of building a calm, cohesive, and visually aligned digital environment that reflects the values of a wellness brand.

challenge.text: Since this project was built from the ground up, the main challenge was defining a clear visual direction without relying on an existing structure. The design needed to communicate calmness, clarity, and trust while organizing different types of content in a way that felt intuitive and balanced. The focus was not only on aesthetics, but on how layout, spacing, and hierarchy could support a more relaxing and understandable user experience.

solution.text: The solution focused on creating a structured layout system that could guide the user naturally through the content. A consistent use of spacing, typography, and color helped reinforce a calm visual rhythm across sections. Each element was intentionally simplified to avoid visual noise, allowing the content to feel more approachable while maintaining a strong and cohesive brand identity.

impact.text: The final result demonstrates how a clear design system can create a cohesive and intentional experience from the ground up. The project highlights decision-making focused on user perception, readability, and emotional tone, showing how design choices can support both brand identity and usability in a wellness-focused environment.

projects.title: Quill Pen Press
projects.subtitle: Webflow
projects.tagline: Brand and one-page website concept for a publishing platform.
projects.summary: Publishing platform concept focused on structure, readability, and brand credibility.

description.text: This project is a brand and website concept for a publishing platform. The goal was to create a credible visual presence that supports readability, content exploration, and a professional identity for writers and readers.

challenge.text: The project was intentionally designed as a single-page website, which forced me to think carefully about how information should flow without overwhelming the user. Instead of relying on multiple pages, I had to prioritize what the user needs to understand first, and how each section would naturally lead to the next. The challenge became less about adding content, and more about controlling hierarchy, pacing, and clarity within a limited space.

solution.text: The solution focused on building a clear visual hierarchy before adding stylistic elements. I started by structuring content into distinct sections, each with a specific role, so the user could scan and understand the site progressively. Typography and spacing were used intentionally to guide attention — larger headings to establish entry points, controlled line lengths for readability, and consistent spacing to create rhythm between sections. Instead of designing visually first, I approached the layout as a system, ensuring that every element had a purpose and contributed to clarity and trust.

impact.text: The final concept communicates a more structured and credible publishing platform. By prioritizing hierarchy and readability, the design supports how users process information rather than relying on visual decoration alone. This approach creates a stronger sense of trust and makes the experience feel intentional, organized, and easier to navigate.

features: Structured content layout
Consistent typography system
Modular section design
Clear visual hierarchy
Responsive layout

testimonials.quote: I started working with Gretel with the idea of creating a website, but I didn't even have a logo. Gretel asked me what idea I had for my logo, and with my idea she made some samples — but she also added her own ideas based on what I was looking for and on her own judgment. After so many examples, I was able to choose a logo much better than my original idea. After the logo, Gretel asked me a series of questions for my website. I gave her only a few details and she was still able to understand me. What's surprising about her, beyond the result, is her willingness to make sure the client is completely satisfied. I would recommend Gretel to anyone, and even more, if I needed services for a logo or a website I would hire her again without any doubt.
